newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil re-election plan left hanging in balance.
newsitem.headline: Brazil re-election plan left hanging in balance.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's plan to run for a second term was left hanging in the balance on Tuesday as the government tried to overcome resistance to re-election within Brazil's biggest party.

A vote on a constitutional amendment allowing re-election was postponed for 24 hours by a Chamber of Deputies committee to give members of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) more time to sort out their differences.
"The ball is in the PMDB's court," Arnaldo Madeira, a whip with Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB), said.

Analysts said the outcome of the struggle between pro- and anti-government wings of the PMDB, Brazil's biggest party, would determine not only whether Cardoso would be allowed to run in 1998 but also the prospects of other proposals to streamline the state during the remainder of his first term. The PMDB has three ministers in Cardoso's cabinet,
"The government has made re-election such a priority that its entire reform programme is practically dependent on it," political analyst Ricardo Pedreira said.
Re-election has been banned since the founding of the republic in 1889 but Cardoso has said he wants a second term to ensure the long-term success of Brazil's new-found climate of economic stability.

Government attempts to approve the re-election measure quickly suffered a blow on Sunday when a PMDB convention dominated by the anti-government wing recommended the party abstain from voting on the issue until Feb. 15.

The crisis appeared to have been resolved on Monday when Cardoso, after urging PMDB leaders to act more like allies than opposition, got a pledge from them to vote on the re-election issue on Tuesday.
But officials later said the PMDB remained too divided to risk a vote on Tuesday. "We'll only vote tomorrow if we're sure of their support," a government spokesman said.
If he loses PMDB support Cardoso can either try to ram the amendment through Congress or rely on his popularity and ask for approval of his re-election bid in a national plebicite.
